If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=3$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{\sqrt{3x-1}-\sqrt{8}} & =\frac{3-3}{\sqrt{3(3)-1}-\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\frac{3-3}{\sqrt{8}-\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{\sqrt{3x-1}-\sqrt{8}} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(\sqrt{3x-1}+\sqrt{8})}{(\sqrt{3x-1}-\sqrt{8})(\sqrt{3x-1}+\sqrt{8})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(\sqrt{3x-1}+\sqrt{8})}{(\sqrt{3x-1})^{2}-(\sqrt{8})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(\sqrt{3x-1}+\sqrt{8})}{3x-1-8} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(\sqrt{3x-1}+\sqrt{8})}{3(x-3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{3x-1}+\sqrt{8}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3(3)-1}+\sqrt{8}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{8}+\sqrt{8}}{3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{8}}{3} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
